title: The First World War
blurb: On 28 June 1914 the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne was assassinated in Sarajevo. By August the Allies, among them Britain, France and Russia, were at war with the Central Powers, Germany and Austria-Hungary. Fighting spread to Africa, Asia and the Pacific, and stopped on 11 November 1918. More than 8.5 million soldiers died, and as many as 13 million civilians.
dateNote: No official body kept count of civilian deaths; the figure is an estimate by historians.

title: Revolution in Russia, depression everywhere
blurb: In 1917 two revolutions shook Russia. The first overthrew the tsar's government and the second brought the Bolsheviks to power; civil war followed until 1922. In August 1929 an economic slump began in the United States and spread around the globe. In Germany it brought mass unemployment and weakened the young republic. In January 1933 Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party came to power.
dateNote: The Depression hit bottom in the United States in March 1933 and dragged on through the 1930s; full recovery came only during the Second World War.

title: From two billion people to eight
blurb: Around 1927 there were two billion people alive. By 1974 there were four billion, and in 2022 the count passed eight billion. The two world wars barely show on the curve. Growth was fastest in the 1960s, at over 2 percent a year. It has slowed since, to under 1 percent a year today.

title: The Second World War and the Holocaust
blurb: Japan had been at war with China since 1937. On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded Poland, and in December 1941 Japan attacked the United States at Pearl Harbor. Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan on 2 September. Some 55 to 65 million people died, most of them civilians. Six million were Jews, murdered by Nazi Germany and its collaborators in the Holocaust.
dateNote: Totals for the war's dead are estimates: the museums cited here give 55 million and over 65 million.

title: The atomic bomb and the Cold War
blurb: On 16 July 1945 the United States exploded the first atomic bomb in the New Mexico desert. In August it dropped two on Japan, killing 90,000 to 166,000 people in Hiroshima and 60,000 to 80,000 in Nagasaki within four months. The Soviet Union tested its own in 1949. In their long rivalry, the Cold War, the world's stockpile passed 60,000 warheads by 1986. The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
dateNote: The number killed by the two bombs is not known precisely: records were destroyed and whole families died.

title: Empires end
blurb: The United Nations began on 24 October 1945 with 51 member states. At that time some 750 million people, nearly a third of humanity, lived in territories ruled by colonial powers. In 1947 British India was divided into India and Pakistan, with great loss of life. By 1960 three dozen new states in Asia and Africa had won independence. The UN now has 193 members.
dateNote: Decolonisation went on after 1960: the UN counts 80 former colonies that have gained independence since 1945.

title: China: revolution, famine and reform
blurb: On 1 October 1949 Mao Zedong declared the People's Republic of China, ending a long civil war. His Great Leap Forward, a drive to industrialise within a few years, forced peasants into communes and into making steel. Harvests collapsed, and between 1959 and 1961 some 30 million people starved. In 1979, less than three years after Mao's death, reformers dissolved the communes and freed farm prices.
debate: Estimates of deaths in the famine run from about 30 million to 45 million. The precise number will never be known.

title: Lives that last decades longer
blurb: A baby born in 1950 could expect, on the world average, to live about 46 years. By 2023 that had risen to 73. Every region gained: Africa went from 37 years to 64, Asia from 42 to 75, and Europe from 62 to 79. The gap between regions narrowed but did not close. The dip in 2020 and 2021 is the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Carbon dioxide: the cost of cheap energy
blurb: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon dioxide, which traps heat in the air. In 1850 the world released about 0.2 billion tonnes a year. By 1950 it was about 6 billion, and in 2024 about 39 billion. Nearly nine-tenths of everything released since 1750 has come since 1950, and more than half since 1990.

title: Into space
blurb: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite: a sphere the size of a beach ball that circled Earth about every 98 minutes. In April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, on a flight of 108 minutes. On 20 July 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin of Apollo 11 walked on the Moon, watched by an estimated 650 million people.

title: The web, and a world online
blurb: In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, working at the CERN laboratory in Geneva, proposed a way to link documents across computer networks. By the end of 1990 the first web server and browser were running, and by October 1993 there were over 200 servers. In 2005 about 16 percent of the world's people used the internet. By 2019 it was more than half, and in 2025 about 74 percent.

title: Fewer in extreme poverty, more who can read
blurb: In 1990, 43 percent of the world's people lived in extreme poverty, which the World Bank defines as less than 3 dollars a day. By 2024 it was about 10 percent, though the pandemic year of 2020 pushed the share up. Reading spread too. About 12 percent of people could read and write in 1820; today more than four in five can.

title: A world of cities
blurb: In 1950 about 29 percent of the world's people lived in towns and cities, going by each country's own definition of urban. In 2007 the share passed half for the first time, and by 2025 it was about 58 percent. The date depends on the definition. Measured by one shared standard that counts towns with cities, most people have lived in urban areas since at least the 1950s.

title: Eight billion
blurb: The United Nations marked 15 November 2022 as the day the world's population reached eight billion. It had taken 12 years to grow from seven billion, and the next billion is expected to take about 15, because growth is slowing. Our species is about 300,000 years old. On the time strip on this story's first page, nearly all of that growth sits in the last thin sliver.
dateNote: The date is a projection: no one can count the world's people to the day.
